title: Does acupuncture work?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether acupuncture works. They open with a 2011 study in the Archives of Ophthalmology (an AMA journal) in which children aged seven to twelve with amblyopia (lazy eye) had better resolution with acupuncture alone than with eye patching. They explain acupuncture in traditional Chinese medicine (qi, yin and yang, meridians, acupoints) and the Western explanation (nervous system stimulation, hormones, neurotransmitters, pain relief). They cover the history from the Huangdi Neijing (around 300 BC) and the Zhen Jiu Da Cheng manual, the 19th-century spread to Europe and France through Georges Soulié de Morant, James Reston's 1971 New York Times account after appendix surgery, and US growth after Nixon's China visit. They describe styles (Japanese, Chinese, five element, auricular/French ear acupuncture, Korean hand acupuncture), moxibustion, electro-acupuncture, and sonopuncture. They walk through a typical session, safety concerns and certification, and clinical studies on knee osteoarthritis, chemotherapy nausea, IVF pregnancy rates, and fibromyalgia, with a skeptical placebo-effect discussion. The episode ends with listener mail about homelessness and a request for surgical horror stories.

segments.title: Opening banter and lazy eye study
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode and discuss amblyopia (lazy eye) and a study in which children with amblyopia improved with acupuncture, with resolution rates compared to eye patching.

segments.title: Chinese and Western explanations of acupuncture
segments.summary: They explain how traditional Chinese medicine describes acupuncture through qi, yin and yang, and meridians with acupoints, and contrast this with the Western explanation of nervous system stimulation and hormone or neurotransmitter release.

segments.title: Origins of acupuncture in ancient China
segments.summary: Acupuncture is traced to Taoist roots and the Huangdi Neijing from about 300 BC, with a later twelve-volume manual, the Zhen Jiu Da Cheng, and early needles made of stone and bone before metal needles.

segments.title: Spread of acupuncture to the West
segments.summary: Acupuncture reached Europe in the nineteenth century, with Georges Soulié de Morant championing it in France. James Reston wrote about his acupuncture treatment in the New York Times, and interest grew in the US after Nixon's China visit. The FDA later classified acupuncture needles as medical instruments.

segments.title: Types of acupuncture
segments.summary: They describe Japanese acupuncture, root and local treatment, five element acupuncture, French auricular (ear) acupuncture with about two hundred points, and Korean hand acupuncture.

segments.title: Moxibustion, electro-acupuncture and sonopuncture
segments.summary: Moxibustion uses heat from burning mugwort (moxa) on acupoints, either directly or indirectly. They also mention electro-acupuncture and sonopuncture, which uses sound instead of needles.

segments.title: What an acupuncture session is like and safety
segments.summary: They describe a typical session with alcohol swabbing, needles inserted a quarter to three inches for 5 to 20 minutes, and a typical course of about twelve weekly sessions. They discuss risks such as organ puncture, bleeding disorders, and pacemakers, and note state regulation and certification hours.

segments.title: Clinical studies and the placebo debate
segments.summary: They review studies on knee osteoarthritis pain, chemotherapy-induced nausea, IVF pregnancy rates with a miscarriage tradeoff, and fibromyalgia. They conclude that skeptics often attribute results to the placebo effect, and argue that understanding the placebo effect is worthwhile.

segments.title: Listener mail on homelessness and a request for surgery stories
segments.summary: Chuck reads responses to the homelessness episode, including a letter from a homeless single mother, and Josh clarifies his criticism of CEOs. They ask listeners to send in stories about wrong-organ surgeries and close with the outro.
